In the grammar session, complete a sentence using the verb shown. In the
affix sessions, learn cue-response pairs and say the paired response.
Say only the answer word, as quickly and accurately as you can.

```{=html}
<div id="priming-app">
  <section id="priming-setup" class="priming-panel">
    <h2>Choose a session</h2>
    <label for="priming-design">Response sets</label>
    <select id="priming-design">
      <option value="grammar">Grammar: shared or mixed grammatical contexts (about 4 minutes)</option>
      <option value="prefix">Prefixes: un-, re-, dis- (about 4 minutes)</option>
      <option value="suffix">Suffixes: -less, -ful, -ness (about 4 minutes)</option>
      <option value="both">Both affix sessions (about 8 minutes)</option>
    </select>
    <label for="priming-measure">How to mark the start of your answer</label>
    <select id="priming-measure">
      <option value="key">Press Space as you begin speaking</option>
      <option value="voice">Microphone: detect sound onset on this device</option>
    </select>
    <p id="priming-measure-help">Space records a manual timing proxy, not a measured speech onset. On a touch device, tap the response button as you begin speaking.</p>
    <p>After each answer, check it against the expected word. Practice trials are not included in the results.</p>
    <button id="priming-start" type="button">Start session</button>
    <p id="priming-setup-status" role="status"></p>
  </section>
  <section id="priming-session" class="priming-panel" hidden>
    <div class="priming-topline"><span id="priming-progress"></span><button id="priming-end" type="button" class="priming-secondary">End session and view results</button></div>
    <div id="priming-stage"></div>
  </section>
  <section id="priming-results" class="priming-panel" hidden></section>
  <noscript>This demonstration needs JavaScript to show cues and record response times.</noscript>
</div>
```

::: {.note}

Microphone mode requests permission only when you start. It detects sound
locally; it does not record, upload, or recognize speech. Background noise can
trigger it. Use a quiet room and check false triggers after each trial.

Session results stay in this page until you download them or leave. Download
the CSV before closing or reloading the page.

:::

<details>
<summary>For discussion after the demonstration</summary>

In **shared** blocks, items share an affix or grammatical context. In **mixed**
blocks, the same items are regrouped so that property varies.
Each item appears twice per measured condition, after practice in each block.
Shared and mixed block order is randomized across sessions.

**Grammar session.** Each trial displays a base verb and a sentence gap,
for example **GO: Yesterday, I ___ home.** Say only **went**. The verbs
are GO, EAT, and BUY in three grammatical contexts:

| Context | Sentence beginning | Responses across the three verbs |
|---|---|---|
| Simple past | Yesterday, I … | went, ate, bought |
| Habitual present | Every day, I … | go, eat, buy |
| Present perfect | I have already … | gone, eaten, bought |

Every block contains all three verbs. Shared blocks use one context; mixed
blocks use all three. For example, a mixed block combines GO in the simple
past, EAT in the habitual present, and BUY in the present perfect. Each
verb-and-sentence combination returns unchanged in both conditions. The
block introduction shows the available contexts and base verbs, without
listing their inflected answers. Answers appear during feedback.

This asks whether knowing the grammatical context helps prepare a response
without a common affix across the three verbs. It is an extension of the
classroom task, not a replication of Roelofs's morphological comparison.
Context reading, repeated sentence frames, and switching between grammatical
contexts can also affect response time. A benefit would not by itself locate
preparation at a particular model stage. The two contexts requiring *bought*
remain separate items, identified by their grammatical features in the CSV.

**Affix sessions.**
The prefix sets are *unkind, unfair, untrue*; *reread, rewrite, repaint*; and
*dislike, distrust, disagree*. The suffix sets are *careless, homeless, hopeless*;
*joyful, helpful, playful*; and *kindness, darkness, softness*. Here, *re-* means
"again"; say *reread* as in "I will reread it."

The preparation benefit is the median correct response time in mixed blocks
minus the median in shared blocks. A positive value means faster responses
in shared blocks. Errors, timeouts, practice, interrupted trials, and responses
under 150 ms are excluded from that timing summary. They remain identifiable
in the CSV. Error counts are reported separately.

These English affix materials are a classroom adaptation, not the materials
from Roelofs's studies. A shared affix also shares sounds and meaning. This demo
has no matched sound-only control, so it cannot establish an extra
**morphological** benefit by itself. The prefix and suffix lists also differ
in frequency, stress, length, and lexical category. Compare each list with
its own mixed baseline; do not treat a prefix-suffix difference as a clean
test of serial position alone.

Roelofs (2000), pp. 98 to 99, reviews the stronger comparison: initial
syllables that constitute morphemes versus initial syllables that do not,
and initial versus non-initial morphemes in implicit preparation.

</details>
